OPEN
This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Let\[F(n) = \max_{\substack{m<n\\ m\textrm{ composite}}} m+p(m),\]where $p(m)$ is the least prime divisor of $m$. Is it true that $F(n)>n$ for all sufficiently large $n$? Does $F(n)-n\to \infty$ as $n\to\infty$?
#385: [Er79d,p.73][ErGr80,p.74]
number theory
A question of Erdős, Eggleton, and Selfridge, who write that 'plausible conjectures on primes' imply that $F(n)\leq n$ for only finitely many $n$, and in fact it is possible that this quantity is always at least $n+(1-o(1))\sqrt{n}$ (note that it is trivially $\leq n+\sqrt{n}$).
Tao has discussed this problem in a blog post.
Sarosh Adenwalla has observed that the first question is equivalent to [430]. Indeed, if $n$ is large and $a_i$ is the sequence defined in the latter problem, then [430] implies that there is a composite $a_j$ such that $a_j-p(a_j)>n$ and hence $F(n)>n$.
See also [463].
Additional thanks to: Sarosh Adenwalla

 Computational note on the first question. The values of $n$ with $F(n)\leq n$ are OEIS A322293 (Michel Marcus and Robert Israel, December 2018), where the search was carried to $10^8$: apart from the trivial $n\leq 4$ there are 100 such $n$, the largest being 267680. The last three values (8742, 267672, 267680) were also found by CKS in the comments on Tao's blog post (August 2024), together with the reduction that every such $n$ is $q+1$ with $q$ prime.
I have extended the search to $10^{11}$ with a segmented least-prime-factor sieve and found no further values, so $F(n)>n$ for all $267680<n\leq 10^{11}$. Since [430] is equivalent to this question, the sequence defined there contains a composite term for every $267680<n\leq 10^{11}$.
Only composites $m>n-\sqrt{n}$ can have $m+p(m)\geq n$ (as $p(m)\leq\sqrt{m}$), which is what makes a sieve to $10^{11}$ cheap: each of ten instances covering $[10^9,10^{11}]$ ran in about a minute. The list of exceptions was reproduced by two independently written programs (to $3\cdot 10^5$ and to $10^6$), and the definition was re-checked directly at 30 random $n$ in $[10^9,10^{11}]$. Code and logs: github.com/leandrejack-afk/erdos-computations.
AI disclosure: the programs were written and run with the assistance of a large language model, and the checks above were run before posting.
 Leandre Jack
